note: Historical leaf-wetness and infection logs display the full available 2022 year, including dates after the selected date of interest. All interpretation for manuscript outcomes is restricted to events before the July 28 rating.
tables: If the post bloom through pea-sized berry period is wet, you are growing susceptible varieties, in hedged vineyards, or locations with a history of Phomopsis, and fungicidal protection is absent, then a final spray for Phomopsis may be needed. The risk of infection is low once berries become about pea-sized (~1/4 inch diam), since inoculum becomes scarce, unless the weather has been very dry for several weeks beforehand. Thus, Phomopsis sprays from this point forward probably are unnecessary in most vineyards.

Berries become highly resistant to infection about 2 weeks (Concord) to 4 weeks (V. vinifera) after fruit set. However, continued foliar protection on Concord (and other American varieties) may be beneficial for heavily-cropped vines or poor-ripening conditions. From this point on, management programs will depend on varietal susceptibility, market destination, ripening conditions, and conducive weather. Secondary infections are favored when cloudy, humid (85% RH), warm (63-86F) days and nights prevail; rain is not required for infection.For V. vinifera and highly susceptible hybrids, maintain protection of the clusters through bunch closure to preclude bunch rots and/or wine spoilage. Maintain an appropriate level of control during the midsummer period to avoid poor ripening, premature defoliation, and reduced winter hardiness.Concord fruit become resistant and no longer require protection. However, in conducive years, foliar protection on Concord and other moderately susceptible varieties may be beneficial for heavily-cropped vines or poor-ripening conditions.Good management will decrease disease pressure next year, by limiting overwintering primary inoculum, reducing spring infection potential, and lowering the risk of cluster infections.

Berries become highly resistant to infection by about 5 (Concord) to 7 (V. vinifera) weeks after the start of bloom. Experience has shown that it is usually possible to end black rot spray programs after the second postbloom application IF the disease has been well managed until then. Scout vineyards for black rot. If black rot symptoms are visible on fruit, fungicide protection to cover infection events through July may be necessary to limit disease spread within clusters.
